modalLead: nextDash is 1.0. After a long stretch of squashing bugs and sanding down rough edges, this finally feels like a finished, stable app rather than a work in progress — so the version number says so. From here the number describes the change instead of the date: 1.x.0 adds features, 1.0.x fixes things. This release is mostly the quiet kind of work: a long list of cases where something claimed to have worked and had not, plus a much stronger Inbox.

sections.title: Things that said they worked and did not

items.text: Moving a bookmark to another page could lose it. If the save half-finished, the bookmark could vanish from both pages at once. It now lands on the new page before it leaves the old one, so a failure leaves it exactly where it started.
Moving several bookmarks at once had the same fault, with the whole batch at risk instead of one. Each is now moved on its own, so one failure cannot take the rest with it.
Deleting all categories on a page appeared to work and changed nothing. It now tells you the bookmarks still filed under them have to be moved first.
Renaming a category could file bookmarks under the wrong one. Deleting a category from the middle of the list shifted the ones after it, quietly moving their bookmarks somewhere you never chose.
A saved link could be silently thrown away. Saving to a full Inbox could discard the very link you just added while reporting success. It is now kept, and the oldest one makes room instead.
Deleting a link during Triage looked like it worked when it had not. The card disappeared and the link came back on the next reload. It now says so instead.

Bulk actions reported partial success as complete success. Snoozing or deleting five links where two failed said everything had gone through. The failures are now named, and Undo no longer restores links that were never deleted.
Deleting a bookmark shown on another page could overwrite other changes made on that page at the same time.
Previews of pages that failed to load were cached as if they had worked, leaving an error page's title on the bookmark.

Tags are finally visible. Links saved with tags — from the browser extension, for instance — showed nothing at all. Tags now appear on the row, you can edit them from the right-click menu, search finds them, and both exports include them. Click one to see only that tag.
Stats. The Stats button answers the question the Inbox is really about: how much of what lands here you turn into bookmarks, and how long things sit before you deal with them.
Promote several links at once. Tick a handful, choose a page, and they all become bookmarks — instead of walking through the form once per link.
Right-click a link and get the Inbox's own actions — Promote, Snooze, Note, Tags, Mark read, Delete — rather than the bookmark menu.
Open and Copy links now sit alongside the other actions when you tick several rows, and Shift+click selects a whole run at once. Ctrl/Cmd+A ticks everything on screen.
An unreachable server said your Inbox was empty and invited you to add to it. It now says the list could not be loaded and offers to try again.
Deleting a row lost your place. Working down the list with the keyboard meant hunting for where you were after every delete; the cursor now moves to the next row.
Filling up the Inbox no longer happens in silence. When an older link is dropped to make room, you are told.
Opening a shared link to one item wiped your search. It also kept dragging you back to that row on every later update.

Bookmarks filed under a category that no longer exists are now findable. Deleting a category leaves its bookmarks behind, and on the dashboard they look no different from uncategorised ones. Health lists them under Missing category and names the one they are still pointing at.
The header is tidier. The score sits on the same line as the description, the trend chart moved down beside the buttons, and settings is a proper button.
The header badge stops hammering a server that is down. It checks less often and backs off when something is wrong, instead of asking every minute forever.
Creating a page and a category at the same moment could undo one of them.
Bookmark names, categories and notes kept any stray spaces you typed around them.
The save hint in the bookmark editor said Ctrl+Enter on a Mac, where it has always been Cmd+Enter.
Copying several links did nothing on some setups — plain-HTTP installs on a home network, in particular.
Deleting several tagged bookmarks at once now offers an Undo, rather than only being recoverable from the 30-day trash.
Smart collection headings could be renamed by accident with a long press or a double click, even though they are not real categories.
Screen readers are told what changed — the Inbox announces how many links a filter leaves, and the buttons that open menus now say that they do.
